issues.legal_issue: A status quo order that specifies the date for preserving the state of affairs refers to the state existing on that date, not to a later state identified during the proceedings.
material_facts: An order concerning the fixed property directed the parties to maintain status quo as of the day the order was made.
A later inventory was taken after a dispute arose about access to and occupation of the property.
issues.conclusion: The status quo to be preserved was the state of affairs on the date of the order, not the state existing when the later inventory was taken.
issues.legal_principle: Status quo means the existing state of things at a given point in time. The Court relied on the definitions in Wharton's Law Lexicon and Black's Law Dictionary, and on Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. v. State of Bihar, which described status quo as the existing state of things at any given point of time.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding alleging disobedience of a court order.
predicates.status_quo_order_specifies_its_reference: The court order identifies the time whose existing state of affairs is to be preserved.
predicates.later_state_is_used_to_interpret_the_ord: A party or court relies on a state of affairs that arose after the specified reference time.

issues.definition: When a contempt proceeding concerns an order that specifies its reference time, and a later state is used to interpret that order, the preserved status quo is the state at the specified time.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot create a sub-tenancy that alters property covered by an existing status quo order, and the sub-tenant cannot obtain an advantage from that act merely because it was not a party to the contempt proceeding.
material_facts: The court had ordered the parties to preserve the status of the fixed property as it existed when the order was made.
An occupant relied on a later agreement to create a sub-tenancy.
The sub-tenant sought to remain in or obtain possession of the property, although the validity of its claimed tenancy was disputed.
issues.conclusion: The later sub-tenancy was contrary to the status quo order and illegal; the sub-tenant could not gain an advantage from it, and the parties were to be returned to the position existing when the order was made.
issues.legal_principle: A status quo order preserving property cannot be circumvented by a later act that changes the preserved state of affairs. The maxim actus curiae neminem gravabit did not apply where the sub-tenancy itself was created in violation of the order. Nor could a person rely on the rule against eviction without due process to obtain an advantage in derogation of the rights of the parties who were already litigating.

rule.if: contempt_proceeding and property_status_quo_order and post_order_subtenancy_created and subtenancy_changes_preserved_property_state

predicates.contempt_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding alleging disobedience of a court order.
predicates.property_status_quo_order: The court order requires the existing state of affairs concerning property to be preserved.
predicates.post_order_subtenancy_created: An occupant creates a sub-tenancy after the property-preservation order is made.
predicates.subtenancy_changes_preserved_property_st: The sub-tenancy changes who occupies or controls the property compared with the state the order preserves.

issues.definition: If a contempt proceeding concerns a property status quo order and an occupant later creates a sub-tenancy that changes the preserved state, that sub-tenancy cannot alter the preserved state and is illegal.

issues.legal_issue: A court considering contempt must confine its orders to the alleged disobedience and cannot use the proceeding to resolve disputed tenancy rights or grant possession to a non-party on an oral request; an appellate court may intervene where such orders exceed that scope.
material_facts: The contempt application alleged interference with access and services to the property in breach of the status quo order.
A company that was not a party to the contempt proceeding made an oral request concerning a padlock and relied on a disputed sub-tenancy.

The courts below made orders concerning the company's occupation and directed that it be allowed to possess the property, although the validity of its claimed tenancy was not for determination in that proceeding.
The appeal challenged those interlocutory orders.
issues.conclusion: The orders concerning the company's occupation and possession were outside the proper scope of the contempt proceeding and were set aside; the contempt court was directed to decide the alleged violation within its proper jurisdiction. The interlocutory nature of the orders did not prevent intervention in these circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: A contempt proceeding alleging breach of an order requires the court to determine whether the order was obeyed. The court must remain within that inquiry and cannot make orders alien to the alleged breach, including orders based on disputed tenancy rights brought before it by an oral request from a non-party. The Court rejected the contention that its practice of not interfering with interlocutory orders barred intervention under Article 136; State of A.P. v. T. Aandagopal and State of Maharashtra v. Dadamiya Babumiya Sheikh had been cited in support of that contention.

predicates.appeal_from_interlocutory_contempt_order: The proceeding is an appeal from interlocutory orders made in a contempt matter.
predicates.contempt_application_alleges_breach_of_a: The contempt application alleges that a party disobeyed an identified court order.
predicates.nonparty_seeks_relief_on_an_oral_request: A person who is not a party to the contempt proceeding asks the court for relief orally.
predicates.challenged_orders_decide_disputed_rights: The challenged orders determine disputed rights or grant relief that is not needed to decide whether the identified order was obeyed.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges interlocutory contempt orders that go beyond deciding an alleged breach by granting relief on a non-party's oral request concerning disputed rights, those orders are set aside and the inquiry is limited to compliance.
